source.name: Doom metal
source.lineage: Doom metal as broad genre family descended from the Black Sabbath template — covering traditional doom (Pentagram, Saint Vitus, Candlemass), funeral doom (the slowest variant, 30-40 BPM, Mournful Congregation, Esoteric, Skepticism), the Electric Wizard / Cathedral UK occult-doom canon, and stoner-doom (psychedelic-sub-elements through Sleep, Electric Wizard, Bongripper) — distinct from the New Orleans sludge-and-hardcore axis covered by sludge metal and distinct from the sustained-tone minimalism covered by drone metal

extras.description: Doom metal (1970 onward, with first-wave English heavy-blues-rock origin through Black Sabbath's eponymous 1970 debut and a 1980s second-wave codification through Saint Vitus, Pentagram, and Trouble), the slow-tempo downtuned-and-sustained heavy metal subgenre. Defined by tempos pushed down to 60-80 BPM with sustained chord-and-riff durations stretching past five minutes, downtuned guitars (D-standard, drop-C, drop-B) producing thicker low-end heaviness, vocal delivery alternating clean-melodic with growled (subgenre-dependent), heavy reverb-and-fuzz guitar tone preserving extended sustain, lyric and visual themes of occult, mortality, and existential dread, and song-form built on slow riff-progression rather than verse-chorus pop structure. Subgenres include traditional doom (clean vocals, heavy-blues), funeral doom (extreme slowness past 40 BPM), and stoner doom (psychedelic sub-elements). Distinguished from heavy metal by tempo; distinguished from drone metal by retention of song-form structure rather than sustained-tone minimalism; distinguished from sludge metal by absence of hardcore-punk-derived aggression and New Orleans regional lineage; distinguished from black-metal atmospheric by absence of blast-beat foundation.

source.name: Stoner metal

extras.description: Stoner metal / stoner rock (codified 1990s onward through Kyuss, Sleep, and Fu Manchu establishing the California-desert sound, with continuous tradition through to present and parallel doom-stoner-and-stoner-rock subgenres), the early-1970s English heavy-blues-rock-derived psychedelic riff music subgenre. Defined by downtuned guitars (drop-C, drop-B, or further detunings) producing thick low-end heaviness, bluesy modal-pentatonic riff vocabulary drawn from Sabbath-and-early-70s heavy-blues-rock heritage, fuzz-and-wah pedal-effected guitar tone with extended sustain, vocal performance often clean-melodic with light-distortion or psychedelic-effected processing, song-form built on extended riff-progression with extended jam-improvisation sections (the Kyuss desert-jam-aesthetic), tempos around 90-120 BPM, and lyric and visual themes addressing cannabis-culture, desert-and-southwest landscape, and psychedelic-mystical experience. Distinguished from straight doom by faster tempo and retention of clean-melodic vocal; distinguished from drone-doom by song-form structure; distinguished from psychedelic-rock by post-1990 timestamp and metal-derived guitar-tone weight.

source.name: Hard rock

Defined by fifth-interval riff vocabulary (the I-V power-chord shape replacing earlier blues-rock's full triadic chord-voicings), shouted-and-wailed high-projection vocal delivery often with blues-rock-derived melismatic ornamentation, concussive bass-drum-and-snare backbeat with prominent fills and tom-foreground percussion, distorted Marshall-stack guitar tone (Big Muff and pre-amp gain-stage saturation), song-forms built on extended verse-chorus with riff-based bridge sections, and tempos around 100-130 BPM. source.name: Grunge

extras.description: Grunge (codified 1985-1995 Seattle and broader Pacific Northwest, with first-wave Sub Pop label era and second-wave major-label commercial breakthrough through Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, and Alice in Chains), the late-1980s/early-1990s hybrid of punk, hardcore, and metal. Defined by Sabbath-derived heavy-blues-rock riff vocabulary translated through hardcore-punk-and-college-rock sensibility, alternation between quiet verse and loud chorus dynamic structure (the soft-loud signature established by the Pixies and adapted), distorted-fuzz-pedal electric-guitar tone (Big Muff fuzz, MXR Distortion+), apathetic-or-distressed vocal delivery, lyric content of generational disaffection, depression, and Pacific-Northwest-suburban-malaise, and college-rock-and-indie-label production aesthetic transitioning into major-label commercial sound 1991 onward. Distinguished from straight metal by punk-and-college-rock lineage; distinguished from hardcore punk by retention of heavy-blues-rock guitar; distinguished from Britpop by US-not-UK origin and darker-and-grungier aesthetic.

Defined by death-metal architecture (downtuned 7- and 8-string guitars, blast-beat percussion, growled vocals) grafted onto metalcore breakdown structure (heavy syncopated chugged-guitar low-tempo breakdowns mid-song designed for moshpit response), alternation between blast-beat sections and breakdown-chug sections rather than continuous metal aggression, vocal delivery alternating death-growl with hardcore-punk pig-squeal and clean-singing chorus sections, and a mid-2000s Hot-Topic-era youth audience and live-show centrality. Distinguished from metalcore by death-metal-not-thrash riff vocabulary and growled-not-shouted vocal; distinguished from death metal by breakdown-structure foreground and clean-vocal chorus; distinguished from slam death metal by hardcore-breakdown rather than groove-metal lineage.

source.name: Acid Rock
source.lineage: San Francisco and Los Angeles psychedelic rock of 1966-1970 codified by the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, Blue Cheer and the 13th Floor Elevators — moderate-tempo blues-derived modal vamps stretched into long extemporised jams, saturated single-coil guitar through fuzz and spring reverb, heavy use of feedback and Leslie-treated organ, wailing declamatory vocals, and a rhythm section that swells and recedes rather than keeping fixed dynamics

extras.description: Acid rock formed on the West Coast ballroom circuit in 1966-67 as bands built extended improvisations over one- or two-chord blues and modal vamps to accompany light shows and long dances. The sound is defined by sustained fuzz and feedback guitar, drifting Leslie organ, chamber and spring reverb applied to whole mixes, and structures that abandon verse-chorus timing for open-ended soloing. It is louder and more blues-pentatonic than the ornate studio psychedelia of British bands, and less song-oriented than garage rock, sitting directly upstream of early heavy metal.
